title: Address tricks
hook: You want to send coins to your friend again. In your wallet history there's an address that starts and ends just like theirs. Copy it?
card1: Scammers send tiny amounts from look-alike [[address|addresses]] so that they show up in your history. This is called address poisoning. If you copy from your history, you might copy theirs.
analogy1: It's like a fake contact saved as "Mum" with almost the same number. One wrong digit, and the call goes to a stranger.
card2: Always get the address from the source: your friend's own message, their wallet's Receive screen, or a contact you saved and checked yourself.
card3: When the amount matters, check more than the first and last four characters, because some look-alikes match both ends. Sending a small test first helps.

history.prompt: Your history shows two addresses: one you paid your friend last week, and one from yesterday that sent you a tiny 0.001 coin you don't remember. Both start with "bb1qx7" and end with "9kd2".

newest.label: Copy the newest one, it's at the top
newest.before: You will copy the top address and send 20 coins.
newest.what: You sent 20 practice coins to the scammer's look-alike address. They're gone.
newest.why: The tiny transaction was bait, to put the fake address at the top of your history.
newest.how: Scammers create addresses that match the first and last characters. The middle is different.
newest.realLife: Never copy an address from your history without checking where it came from.

compare.label: Compare the first and last characters
compare.before: You will check both ends of each address.
compare.what: Both match. You still don't know which one is real.
compare.why: Look-alike addresses are made to pass exactly that check.
compare.how: Matching a few characters at each end is easy for a scammer's computer.
compare.realLife: When both ends match, check the middle too, or get the address fresh.

ask.label: Ask your friend to send their address again
ask.before: You will ask your friend for their address directly.
ask.what: Your friend sent it. It matches last week's, not yesterday's. You sent the coins safely.
ask.why: Getting the address from the source beats any memory or history.
ask.how: The odd 0.001 transfer came from a stranger, not from your friend.
ask.realLife: Save checked contacts in your wallet and ignore tiny unexpected transfers.

q1.a: Scammers put a look-alike address into your history
q1.b: A virus that breaks your wallet
q1.explanation: Tiny transfers from look-alike addresses try to trick you into copying the wrong one later.

q2.prompt: Where is the safest place to get a friend's address?
q2.b: From your friend directly, or a contact you saved and checked
q2.explanation: Get it from the source every time, or from a contact you checked yourself.

q3.prompt: You receive 0.001 coins from an address you don't know. What should you do?
q3.b: Ignore it and never copy that address
q3.explanation: Tiny unexpected transfers are often bait. Ignore them and don't interact.

misc.poisonVirus: "It's a virus." Address poisoning needs no virus. It just tricks you into copying the wrong address.
misc.poisonBlock: "The blockchain gets poisoned." The blockchain is fine. Only your history gets a fake entry.
misc.historyCopy: "My history is safe to copy from." Scammers can put look-alike addresses there.
misc.searchAddr: "I can find the address online." Search results can be faked. Ask your friend.
misc.sendBack: "Send it back to be nice." That's what they want: interacting puts their address in your history again.
misc.smallGift: "It's a small gift." Tiny unexpected transfers are usually bait.

t1: Look-alike [[address|addresses]] can match the first and last characters.
t2: Get the address from the source, not from your history.
t3: Ignore tiny unexpected transfers and save contacts you have checked.
talk1: Have we ever saved a wrong phone number or email? How did we notice?
talk2: How could you check an address with a friend in a way a scammer couldn't fake?
